1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2.strategy: The natural completion of the fianchetto: the bishop looks down the long diagonal at the centre and the queenside, and White can castle next. It commits to a flexible, patient set-up in which White builds behind the pawns and chooses the central plan later.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3.strategy: Prepares a second fianchetto, with a bishop on b2 as well, so that both bishops eye the centre from a distance. The pawn on b3 weakens nothing urgent, but White gives up some flexibility: the set-up is aimed at the long diagonals rather than at the centre pawns.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b4.strategy: Grabs queenside space at once and prepares the bishop for b2, behind the pawn on the long diagonal. The cost is that the b-pawn stands undefended and can be challenged by Black's queenside pawns, while the kingside pieces are still at home: ambitious, but second-rate.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b4.name: King's Indian Attack: Smyslov Variation

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7.strategy: Black completes the fianchetto in the same way: the bishop presses on the centre from the long diagonal and the king is ready to castle behind the g6 pawn. A solid, symmetrical answer that makes the second white fianchetto no threat.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7.strategy: Black mirrors White: the bishop takes the long diagonal and aims at the centre, and the king can castle next. A symmetrical, solid answer that keeps all central options open and leads to a patient game of manoeuvring.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7 4.Bb2.strategy: Finishes the queenside fianchetto: the bishop eyes the knight on f6 and the e5 square, and with the king's bishop to come White controls the centre from a distance instead of occupying it. The game stays quiet and manoeuvring, with the pawn breaks still to be chosen.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7 4.Bb2 O-O.strategy: Black tucks the king away behind the fianchetto pawns and lets White show the plan. Nothing is conceded in the centre, and the rook on f8 gets ready to support a later pawn advance there.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7 4.Bb2 O-O 5.B.strategy: Completes the double fianchetto: both bishops now bear on long diagonals, and castling is White's next step. The set-up asks Black to find a plan, since White has not yet committed a single central pawn.

A solid reply: the pawn on d6 holds the e5 square and frees the c8-bishop, while Black keeps every plan open for the middlegame. It is less direct than a claim on the centre, but it leaves nothing to attack.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7 4.Bb2 O-O 5.B.name: Zukertort Opening: Double Fianchetto Attack
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7 4.Bb2 O-O 5.B.strategy: Finishes the development of the set-up and safeguards the king. From here the game is a slow manoeuvring struggle: the central squares are held by pieces, and whichever side prepares its pawn break better gets the more active play.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O.strategy: White tucks the king away behind the fianchetto and completes the kingside development before deciding on the central plan. The move commits to a closed, strategic game in which White builds slowly and keeps the choice of pawn structure.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O O-O.strategy: Black does the same: the king is safe, the position is fully symmetrical, and neither side has yet committed a central pawn. The fight is for who sets the agenda with the next pawn move.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O O-O 5..strategy: Supports the squares e4 and c4 with a modest pawn and frees the queen's bishop, building the flexible set-up in which White later plays for a central advance with the e-pawn. Slow, but it keeps the position solid.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O O-O 5..name: King's Indian Attack: Wahls Defence
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O O-O 5..strategy: Black claims central space at once with a pawn that also controls e4 and c4, denying White's e-pawn its easy advance. In return the structure is committed, and the game stays level and strategic, both sides playing for pawn breaks.
